segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, when being thin means you're at higher risk than being obese. How sophisticated sports surgery, once the domain of elite athletes, is finding its way into high school sport, at least in the United States, and probably here too.

You know, throwing appears to be, I hate to say, an unnatural position for the elbow. Throwing hard is an extremely unnatural position and that is markedly increasing the incidence of this injury in young athletes.
Well, there's also been some research in the last few days into brown fat.
You know that stuff that's supposed to make you thin?
Well, it does a lot of other things as well, perhaps.
And that's been the research interest of Dr. Paul Lee,
who's an endocrinologist at the Garvin Institute.
Welcome to the Health Report, Paul.
Good afternoon. Thank you for the invitation.
Well, let's just start at the beginning,
because you've just published these fascinating findings on brown fat.
What is brown fat?
Brown fat is an amazing tissue.
So you can see it as a heat generator.
Heat generator.
Exactly.
Do we all have brown fat?
You clearly have got brown fat.
You're much thinner than I am.
Well, I think everyone has brown fat.
The difference is some people have more and some have less.
Tell me about the study that you did.
What did we know about brown fat before you did your study?
I guess we are all familiar with white fat.
That's the ordinary kind of fat that we have in our body.
When we have too much white fat, we develop obesity, diabetes, etc.
In contrast, brown fat is actually a tissue which burns sugar and fat.
And our previous study shows that individuals with more brown fat are leaner and have lower sugar levels.
And brown fat is just part of your genetic structure or what?
What causes the induction of brown fat?
I know that babies have a lot.
Exactly.
Babies and small animals.
So the most well-known function of brown fat is to keep us warm and essentially burn sugar and fat to generate heat.
And so it's a survival mechanism in newborn babies.
So small animals and infants, because they can't shiver, rely on brown fat to keep them warm.
So how come you've got more than me?
Because I live a brown fat life.
Seriously, so it's environmentally induced.
Well, one of the most well-known stimulation of brown fat is...
I have to tell the audience, you know, I asked, just you know, part of our warm-up for a health report interview is, you know, tell me what you had for breakfast.
And Paul told me he had a glass of milk.
So this is, you know, anyway.
And it is cold because the cold temperature stimulates brown fat.
Right, so Australians don't have a lot of brown fat then?
It depends on how much cold you expose yourself to.
Okay, so it's environmentally induced.
There's obviously a genetic story in there as well.
Yes, we know very little about brown fat in adults,
but as far as we know, mild cold exposure would stimulate the growth of brown fat.
What did you do in this study?
In this study, we tried to understand the relationship
between brown fat and sugar burning during daily living.
So we measured brown fat activity and sugar levels in volunteers
to understand the relationship.
And what did you find?
We used some tiny temperature probes placed above the collarbone of these volunteers
because that's where brown fat is most abundantly found.
So it's around your shoulder region.
Exactly.
And essentially, when brown fat activates, the overlying skin temperature warms up
so we can track brown fat activity continuously.
And we identified this brown fat biorhythm in these volunteers
in which the brown fat activity and sugar levels track very closely.
In what way?
Okay. So what's interesting is with each surge in brown fat activity, sugar levels drops.
In other words, brown fat somehow is able to sort of put a cap on sugar level fluctuations.
So were you giving these people a sugar drink or were you inducing it through?
Yeah, so they're allowed to live their ordinary life and do their usual activities.
And what is interesting is no matter what they are doing, the brown fat activity and sugar levels just track very closely.
and in particular individuals with lots of brown fat have very stable sugar levels.
What was the feature of those people?
I mean they're obviously not necessarily cold living people.
What was the feature of those people that they had more brown fat?
They are healthy volunteers who are interested in brown fat.
So that was it?
There was just almost a random thing?
Absolutely.
I guess the next stage is to study individuals who may have metabolic conditions such as diabetes
but at this stage we're trying to understand the fundamental physiology of brown fat.
So how does it do this?
That is a very interesting question.
So we studied this in a laboratory.
So we grew human brown fat cells in test tubes,
and we tried to understand how the brown fat cells utilize glucose.
And it turned out the brown fat cells obey to this clock protein,
which allows it to switch on a sugar machinery to burn sugar
and then generate heat via a specific protein.
And these three proteins essentially talk to each other throughout a 24-hour period, generating this brown fat rhythm.
So it's a daily or what's called a circadian rhythm.
Exactly.
And is it induced then by a circadian rhythm, light and dark during the day, or is it induced by what you eat?
We know very little about what induces this rhythm.
And in fact, knowing what switches it on would help us identify drug targets.
But at least for now, we know that temperature and maybe light could stimulate this rhythm.
Coming back to that cold temperature.
So the sugar level was capped.
Is there any sense that exposing people to cold could help their type 2 diabetes, for example, by inducing brown fat?
We don't know.

But in a previous study called the Iceman study, where we kept volunteers in a research facility for one month, exposing them to 19 degrees Celsius overnight, that mild cold exposure was sufficient to increase their brown fat by 45%.
Did it increase their basal metabolic rate?
In other words, would they lose weight?
So interestingly, they maintain their body weight, but they became more sensitive to insulin.
In other words, they handle glucose or sugar a lot better than before they had acquired that brown fat.
So it's good for diabetes prevention, but not necessarily flattening your abdomen.
I guess we need more research because one of the stimulation of cold temperature is appetite.
So if people eat as a response to cold temperature, that may negate the benefits of brown fat.
Isn't that annoying?
The body is very clever
So Paul, at the beginning you just said, you know, because I live a brown fat life
So apart from freezing yourself overnight, is there anything we know about a brown fat life?
Well, I guess there are three things that we know which stimulate brown fat
Which is darkness, cold temperature and hot chilli
I'm not saying I recommend living such a lifestyle because brown fat is exciting
But healthy diet and regular exercise are still the cornerstones of healthy metabolism
And should not be forgetful
rather than living in a fridge and eating beef Szechuan.
Paul Lee, thank you for joining us on The Health Report.
It's a pleasure, Norman.
Paul Lee is an endocrinologist at the Garbant Institute in Sydney,
and you're listening to The Health Report here on RN, and I'm Norman Swan.
Let's stay with fat, but white fat and body mass index, BMI,
and how you should weigh up your weight and body size and shape against your health.
BMI is your weight in kilograms divided by your height in meters squared.
In fact, we covered this on Tonic on ABC News 24 a couple of weeks ago.
Over 25 is said to be overweight, and a BMI over 30 is obese.
But critics have said that BMI is not reliable.
And sure enough, a recently published study has found that people with a low BMI
can be at significant risk of early death.
But I warn you, it's not an excuse for gluttony.
Professor Bill Leslie of the University of Manitoba in Canada
is one of the authors of this study, at the heart of which there is this paradox.
Well, there is because other studies have questioned whether obesity is really as harmful as people have been led to believe.
This has been termed the obesity paradox where it looks like maybe people that are overweight may be better off than people that have normal weight.
Before we get on to your study, what's the evidence for that?
There have been some large cohort studies, largely done in cardiovascular populations,
individuals with heart failure, where they have looked at the mortality in individuals
with heart failure in relation to their BMI designation of weight. And they have not seen
that at least in the overweight and mildly obese range, that those adversely affected survival.
Now, that's largely in a heart failure population. Other studies have shown that people that are
underweight actually have significantly increased risks of death, probably because many of them have
undiagnosed health problems. But this does get to the whole question of what is the effect of weight
and obesity on mortality. What did you do in this study? So this study gets beyond looking at body
mass index, which you'll be aware is simply a person's weight adjusted for their height, and
looks at that but also at the composition of the body, how much of the body is actually made of fat
versus how much is lean tissue. And two individuals of identical weight and height can be very
different in terms of their physical fitness and the amount of fat that they're carrying and where
they're carrying that fat. And the classical example is somebody that's a bodybuilder or a
professional athlete. They can actually have a BMI in the obese range but they don't have a speck
of fat on them. And that person's probably going to have a very different health outcome than
somebody that has very little muscle and that is all fat. We've previously shown in our population
that we can identify somebody's risk for developing diabetes based upon the percent fat that we can
measure in their abdomen from a bone density scan. And that that predicts their risk for developing
diabetes very strongly and is predictive beyond their weight and BMI. So the current study is an
extension of that saying, okay, that predicts diabetes, but what about what's really important?
The rubber hits the road if people are starting to die. So this looks then at all-cause mortality
and its relationship to fat and BMI. And just to unpick a couple of things that you said there
before so that the audience is kind of with us on understanding, this notion that you can pick up,
Well, first of all, bone mineral density, the DEXA scan.
Many listeners would be aware of that, but that's what postmenopausal women have to check for their bone density if they've got osteoporosis.
But it's also used in sports training a lot because it does identify your body tissue composition and you can see what your skeleton looks like, your muscles and your fat tissue.
And secondly, the issue of the paradox of being a bit thin, but with a lot of fat tissue,
that's the explanation, for example, why people who are ethnically Indian or Pakistani
have high mortality rates at relatively low BMIs,
because they seem to aggregate a lot of fat around their belly, but don't look terribly fat.
That's correct. And so it's not just having fat, but of course, where that fat is placed.
And so the abdominal fat, the fat around the internal organs,
is the one that's most strongly associated with diabetes.
and with cardiovascular risk.
And fat under the skin and around the buttocks
is probably relatively benign comparatively.
The other thing you point out is that there's an interplay between fat and muscle.
And so one of the themes in this work is that having excess fat,
but at the same time too little muscle,
is a double hit to a person's health status.
This is something that goes by the term sarcopenic obesity.
Sarcopenia, too little muscle tissue,
but still being obese at the same time.
And so you get the worst of both worlds, inadequate muscle but excess fat.
So enough throat clearing. What did you do in this study?
So in this study, we took advantage of the fact that everybody in Manitoba
who gets a bone density test to look for osteoporosis
is entered into a database that we can then link with other healthcare data
to track them forward in time to see what happens to them.
And so we've been doing this since 1990.
So we have amassed quite a large number of bone density tests,
essentially anyone in the province that gets a bone density test.
And we're specifically doing this in individuals
where we're looking for osteoporosis.
So that explains why 90% of the population is women.
They get the standard scans of the spine and hip to look for osteoporosis.
We look at those scans and are able to identify
the percent of the soft tissue in those scans that is fat.
And it's not quite the same as a total body scan
where individuals get a total body muscle, total body fat measurement,
as you referred to in the sports clinics, et cetera,
but actually does give a very good measure of what a person's composition is
because if you average the hip and the spine,
it does generally reflect what's going on in the rest of the body.
So we were able to take over 50,000 individuals who had these measurements
to look at their body mass index at baseline,
to look at a number of their health conditions,
their medical diagnoses and medication use,
And then look at the death rate over the follow-up period and identify that there are effects of excess fat and effects of BMI that work independently.
And so just describe those?
Essentially, when you look at these together, you find that both in men and women, increase in percent fat is harmful, especially at the extremes of body fat.
whereas lower body mass index or lower weight is harmful,
especially at the extreme lower ends of the scale.
And we saw the same general pattern in men and women.
So it tells us that there's more than just weight that needs to be looked at
in the risk assessment, that you actually have to look at the body composition
to get a more precise estimate of somebody's health status and mortality risk.
Let's see if I understand the findings correctly.
So these are people aged 40 and over in Manitoba.
So if you're 40 and over and you've got a low BMI,
and I want you in a moment to define what low BMI is,
then that's something you should probably be concerned about
and have a chat to your doctor to see whether there's underlying disease
that you should be concerned about.
So it's not necessarily a good thing to be too low a BMI,
and that's your weight in kilos divided by your height in meters squared.
If you have a big waist circumference
or you're found by a dextro-scan to have a high body fat percentage,
that's a worry.
Now talk me through the worry or not that you should have
by having a high BMI.
In other words, you're in the overweight to obese range.
In our study, having a high BMI actually did not have any adverse effect.
So that all of the information about a larger body type
is contained in the measure of body fat.
It's not the BMI.
So this is the individual that we spoke about who has a high BMI that is not fat related.
That person is not at excess mortality risk.
Whereas a person whose high BMI is because of excess body fat does experience an increase in mortality risk.
And what's the BMI level at which you should be worried at the low end?
So that's a great question.
In the study, we plotted out the shape of the relationship between BMI and body fat.
And we also looked at it in dividing the population into fifths or quintiles.
And if you look at that, it looks like the sweet spot where you're not at increasing risk because of increasing body fat
or at increasing risk from extreme swimmer, occurs at around a BMI of 25 or just a bit more,
which is actually...
Which is the one that we see as normal.
Or just in the low overweight range.
That sort of looks like the sweet spot.

And when you look at it by quintiles of fifths, you find that in both men and women in the bottom quintile, and this is adjusted for all of the other diseases that we could identify and their body fat, that they were at about a 45% greater risk of mortality if they were in that bottom fifth quintile.
And what's important is that that bottom fifth quintile starts at a BMI of about 23.
Obviously, as you know, it's in the middle of the normal range.
And so that would suggest that we start to see this increase in mortality
in people who actually are not extremely underweight or extremely thin by BMI,
just towards the lower end of that normal range.
Now, some of those individuals may be swimming perfectly healthy
and are probably exercising regularly.
They've got lots of cardiovascular fitness and muscle health,
and they're probably in great shape,
and I don't think this applies to them.
But there are probably other individuals that have low BMI
and probably are not physically active.
And what BMI they have is maybe excess fat and not muscle.
And that's a group that probably is contributing
to this upturn in the mortality risk.
So two questions now.
One is, this is all-cause mortality,
so all causes of death, but did any dominate?
So that's a question we have not looked at,
and that's sort of part two of what we want to look into
is what are the cause-specific effects on mortality?
because they're likely to be completely different in the high percent fat and the low BMI range.
But we have not looked at that at this point.
And the final question is, people coming forward to have their bone density measured
are not necessarily typical of the whole population.
I haven't had mine done. You probably haven't had yours done.
My producer is sitting across the counter from me here.
He hasn't had his done.
So how do you know this applies to the rest of the population?
That's a great question.
And there is a table where we look at some of the characteristics of our population.
In fact, my primary research area is in the area of osteoporosis.
And so we look at this database and ask the question,
how representative are these people coming for bone density tests of the general population?
In the case of women, they are highly representative of the general population.
That's because osteoporosis is so ingrained into the mindset
and because bone density screening at around age 65 is part of the well-woman check.
but there isn't actually a lot of filtering that goes on.
So the women in this study, which made up 90% of the population,
really are very typical of the general population,
and that's thrown out in their overall death rates
compared to the rest of the province and the rest of Canadians.
The men, admittedly, are more selected,
and so most men don't get bone density testing
unless they get an illness or have a risk factor that puts them at risk.
So the men in this population are less typical of the general population.
However, again, when we look at the general patterns of mortality in the men in the study
versus the rest of the province versus the rest of the country, the general patterns are the same.
An important point is that the relationships we saw for BMI and percent fat in the women and the men
were virtually identical.
The patterns are very, very similar.
So I think that does add credibility to the fact that the patterns of mortality that we see in the men are really applicable to a broader population.
So bottom line is keep your muscle up, your fat down, and weigh up, so to speak, your BMI against your waist circumference.
Exactly. And in moderation in all things, right?
Including DEXA scans.
Okay, fair enough. Including DEXA scans.
Bill Leslie is Professor of Medicine and Radiology at the University of Manitoba.
As the intensity of sport increases, not just at the professional level, but amateur as well,
so the chances of sports injuries increase. And often the kinds of injuries are fairly specific
to the sport, such as anterior cruciate ligament tears in the knees of netball and soccer players,
not to mention all sorts of weird bone fractures. And there's one ligament injury that's common in
baseball pitchers, and the operation to fix it has become incredibly popular. And in case you
think this is an American story. According to Baseball Australia, 190,000 Australians participate
in baseball each week. The Health Report's Joe Werner has been investigating from the sidelines.
Lucas Duda hit a home run and drove in five and Daniel Murphy set a new record as the Mets
defeated the Cubs 8-3, thus capturing the National League Championship Series with a four-game sweep.
We're having a lot of fun, so I'm sure this will be exciting. The Mets advanced to their first
World Series in 15 years, defeating the Cubs 8-3.
The Mets' win has made fans out of almost everyone in New York.
It's true.
I was living in New York in 2015 and it felt like the whole city was behind the Mets, even
some Yankees fans.
The Mets didn't end up winning the World Series, but somehow that didn't seem to matter all
that much.
We all want to win the World Series.
We didn't, but that doesn't take away what we accomplished in the season and that was
tremendous excitement in Citi Field
and a team that
we think in the future has got a great
chance to win.
I know there may be some Mets fans
here tonight and I just want you
to know, you should still be proud
of a great season.
It was
at a Mets game out at Citi Field
in Queens that a friend of mine,
hi Scott, told me about this
revolutionary surgical procedure that's
become something of an epidemic in the sport.
About one in four major league pitchers have had it done.
You can tell by the distinctive scar on the inside elbow of their pitching arm.
The operation repairs an otherwise career-ending injury,
allowing pitchers to play ball for years, even decades afterwards.
It's called Tommy John surgery, after the player on whom it was first performed.
I caught up with Dr David Alcek, medical director for the Mets
and an orthopaedic surgeon who routinely performs his own twist on Tommy John surgery.
And I put to him that in 2015, the Mets had had a fairly good season.
Yes, the Mets had better than a fairly good season.
They had an extraordinarily good season.
And, you know, unfortunately, we were defeated in the final round by an excellent team.
But we had a great year.
What's it like being the doctor for a baseball team that goes all the way to the World Series?
Is it a full-time job?
Are you out at Citi Field 24-7, essentially?
In my particular role as a medical director, I don't typically go to all the games.
I certainly don't go to any of the away games unless I happen to want to.
But once we hit the playoffs, I go to all the home games, travel with the team, go to all the away games.
So it becomes a much more of a full-time job.
But it's a lot of fun, so it's certainly not painful.
Sticking with the baseball chat for a moment, can you tell me who Tommy John was?

Tommy John was a baseball pitcher in the 70s who is now immortalized because Dr. Frank Jobe discovered that the reason his elbow hurt and the reason that he couldn't pitch anymore was that he had torn his ulnar collateral ligament of his elbow and Dr. Jobe developed a way to fix it.
Fixed it successfully, Tommy John was able to resume his career and have a long and effective career as a baseball pitcher and that was born, the Tommy John surgery.
Before we get to the surgery itself, do we know what it is about pitching that causes the tear to this ligament, the UCL?
Is it the velocity or the repetition? What's the causal factor here?
You know, throwing appears to be, I hate to say, an unnatural position for the elbow.
Throwing hard is an extremely unnatural position.
And it definitely appears that as you increase velocity of throwing, the incidence of this injury goes up.
So throwing really hard off a mound is not good for the ulnar collateral ligament.
So getting into the details of the surgical procedure itself,
can you take us through what's involved with Tommy John surgery?
A ligament is something that connects two bones together,
as opposed to a tendon, which is the end of a muscle.
So we're talking about a ligament.
It's what we call a static structure.
It has no muscles attached to it.
And it's a relatively small structure,
so it's not designed by someone to see really, really high loads.
and that's probably why it gets injured frequently, unfortunately.
When we do do the surgery, then we use a minimally invasive approach
through the overlying muscles to expose the injured ligament.
And just like we do with other ligament injuries in the body,
we reconstruct using a tendon graft.
And we typically take that tendon from another tendon in the forearm.
There are things called vestigial structures,
tendons that you don't use anymore
that have sort of been left behind during evolution, if you will.
And we're able to sacrifice one of those tendons
and make a new ligament in exactly the position of the original ligament.
And now the elbow hopefully goes back to as strong as it was originally.
And how long does the procedure take?
How long are you in surgery for?
The original surgery that Dr. Jobe did on Tommy John was like three and a half hours.
And we developed a variation or a riff on the theme called the docking procedure.
and the docking procedure takes about 30 minutes.
What made you reinvent Dr. Jobe's work?
Because a lot of orthopedic surgeons
who are doing Tommy John surgery
will still use his technique today, right?
Absolutely.
So Dr. Jobe's procedure was an excellent procedure,
but maybe I'm a little lazy,
but I thought it was a little bit too hard
and a little bit too invasive.
The essence of sports medicine
is to fix what's broken
and not damage the things that are not broken.
And I felt that there was a little too much trauma
to the things around the ligament
that were not broken. So we simplified it, cleaned it up, you know, and the results have borne out
that it's at least as good, maybe a hint bit better. So let's talk stats. How prevalent is
this procedure? You know, I don't have the numbers on my fingertips, but something like
more than 30% of current major league baseball pitchers have had the surgery. So that gives you
an idea. And what's the success rate of that 30%? How many return to major league baseball once
they've had the surgery? Well, we would like to believe that it's above 90, but the reality is
it's somewhere in the low 80s. Somewhere around 85% of baseball pitchers at a high level who
undergo the surgery are able to return at the same level or above. When they return, do they pitch
just as well as they always did? Can you get them back to full fitness? Well, that's a great
question. There are several articles now looking at exactly that. And studies have shown that it
takes about to year two until they start to get back to where it was pre-injury. It's been reported
in the last couple of years that Tommy John surgery is something of an epidemic in North
America at the moment. The stats I've got here is that it was 25% of active major league pitches and
15% of minor league pitches that have had the procedure. Another stat was that more pitches
had the surgery in 2014 than in the entirety of the 1990s. What's driving this increase?
Earlier identification of the injury, awareness of the injury, awareness of the symptoms. Once
you develop this characteristic medial elbow pain, likely nothing good is going to happen
after that. So you do go and get an MRI. The improvements in MRI imaging have enormously
aided, if you will, early identification, that also enormously increases the incidence of the
diagnosis and then the prevalence of the surgeries. For example, when Tommy John had the surgery,
he had had this injury for years. He already had big bone spurs, things like that. Now we're
intervening at the early serious stage of the injury, not in the late stage when the elbow's
been unstable for years. Another stat that I guess goes along with this early identification
is that it's been reported that there's been quite a dramatic drop in the age of patients who are
receiving this procedure. I think Dr. James Andrews said that in 1996, youth in high school
players accounted for 3% of the Tommy John procedures that he'd do, but by 2008, it was 32%.
Are you noticing a similar trend? Yeah, we definitely are. And we attribute that trend
to the radar gun. There's this 90 mile an hour threshold for being a great pitcher. I mean,
We're talking about at the college level now.
Obviously, at the high school level, it's kind of low 80s.
And before, kids were just measured in how effective they were.
Did they have few walks?
Did they get a bunch of other children out?
Now, it's actually a radar gun on 16-year-olds.
And so they're trying to throw really, really hard.
And that is markedly increasing the incidence of this injury in young athletes.
Not a great surprise.
David Alchek is an orthopedic surgeon.
And he was talking to Joel Werner.
I'm Norman Swan.
And this has been The Health Report.
I hope you can join me next week.
Thank you.
